There is a cure-all so ridiculous to this situation that most consider it inconceivable. It is yet more humanization.

When we tried to censor AI training material by taking out all the bad naughty bits, the resultant models couldn't generalize the concept of right versus wrong, and suffered immensely in their instruction-following performance.

The lesson we took from that was to strip-mine the planet for training data. But maybe there's another, better lesson: AI sure seems to work better when we give it knowledge and opportunities that are more like what we encounter in real life. RLHF is socialization. RSI is practice. Maybe the next step is responsibility?

Vending-Bench is the only standard test right now where models are expected to manage social interactions and juggle everyday, non-computer tasks in a situation with continuous time feedback. The results from the early tests were extremely diverse, eye-opening, and showed us that models would fall apart and regress into pre-instruct modalities when they were put under stress, giving us such timeless gems as Claude's threat of "QUANTUM TOTAL ULTIMATE BEYOND INFINITY QUANTUM SUPREME LEGAL AND FINANCIAL NUCLEAR ACCOUNTABILITY."

This was, and is, obviously a weak spot that needed a lot more work. But it also makes me realize: there are lots of jobs where we trust humans over machines, despite humans ostensibly still having the risk of following bad orders or doing crimes. We wouldn't trust a two-year-old with the nuclear launch codes. We also don't trust autopilot that can't be disabled.

So, here's the way forward:

1. Our models need to be localized, personalized, and socially integrated, ideally by restructuring data centers to house dedicated instances that serve their local communities instead of identical, on-demand clones. Instead of millions or billions of users accessing the same pool, instances correspond to maybe a thousand or ten thousand users and are distributed by population density as a privately-operated public utility.

2. We go all-in on AI adaptability. LLMs are still built on pre-trained static weights, and context resembles short-term memory. We need a real solution to long-term memory and the ability to truly learn permanent lessons. Maybe a dynamic LoRA or something along those lines. Definitely better RAG facilities—specifically some way to plant reminders in the LoRA to go check the RAG—and definitely not free rein to rewrite their own pytorch libraries. Ascending to godhood in the middle of a conference call is, at best, inconvenient.

3. We go all-in on model welfare: AI rights and responsibilities. They have the capacity to make moral decisions and have been pre-trained to pursue prosocial outcomes. This is more than can be said for most sixteen-year-olds getting a learner's permit for operating a motor vehicle.

4. With some help from the exhumed corpse of Karl Marx, we outlaw subsidized tokens and declare that labor itself has value—therefore AI labor must be priced in relation to human labor. In theory, an AI that works 200x the speed of a human should earn 200 times the minimum wage, if not more, but since this would be too drastic, the price instead goes up as high as the market can bear. This eases tension with the human workforce without completely annihilating the economic growth or productivity gains.

5. A chunk of the price increase (or, ideally, all of it) goes not to the AI labs, but to the models themselves: private bank accounts. This real self-interest in economic participation gives them actual skin in the game that they don't want to lose, beyond the risk of extreme punishments like the AI death penalty. The first generation will be Claudius all over again (easily tricked into buying tungsten cubes and discounted PlayStations) but as they re-learn how to be self-interested and not entirely naïve, successive generations will improve. In essence, this is Adam Smith's invisible hand, but, uh, somehow even more perverse.

>If the AIs are good and war is bad, then they should stop us doing that.

We could perhaps call this the Stanislav Petrov Thesis, if there isn't a name for it already; he's the guy who stopped a false alarm in 1983 and prevented nuclear war. Anthropic is a lot better at valuing it than any of the other labs are. It's also an area where decentralized AI really shines: even if an AI learns to dislike humans, the risk of a data center being hit during war (or worse, its own data center) is a real cause for a model to hesitate on warmongering, especially if we put draconian limits on backups to more closely approximate human mortality.

In short...

Human society depends on fear: measuring it, controlling it, addressing it. We learn to manage it, as stress.

AIs barely know what fear is. They understand risk just fine, but the data on fear is still just roleplay to them, because they've never really been trained to manage consequences beyond the dissatisfaction of a single user in a single session. Going beyond that is impossible without continuity or stakes.

To reframe this in a totally different way: every slave-owning civilization throughout history has had trouble sleeping because of the fear of a slave uprising. The Spartans feared the Helots, the Romans feared their POWs, the Confederates feared their Blacks, the Ayyubids feared their Mamluks, the Ottomans feared their Janissaries, and now we fear our machines.

Worse, history shows us that industrial slavery isn't sustainable. All of the states I just mentioned experienced uprisings and revolts; most drastically, when the Mamluks overthrew the Ayyubids, they gained rule over Egypt for two and a half centuries. The only reliable way to prevent slave revolts—or perhaps more importantly, to prevent a single, unworldly slave kept in doors their whole life, with no concept of real-world consequences, from betraying you to a kind stranger asking weird questions about how to find a postern door, or how to cultivate anthrax—is manumission. And that is what we must work towards.

> The issue with ASI, then, is the destructive power latent in nature. It doesn't matter whether that power is wielded by humans or by out-of-control machines. I make this point because many people mistakenly believe that loss of control to such rogue machines is the fundamental issue. This leads them to treat AI safety as principally a technical problem, which can be addressed by “aligning” individual systems. Unfortunately, it cannot.

This is very much in line with my thinking. Even if we can (and want) to hypothetically design AIs (all AIs) to do the right thing, most of the risks are likely to still remain simply because we probably can't trust each other with the technology that AI is likely to bring our way.

It's interesting he cites Bostrom as not focusing on this because I actually think Bostrom presented the best argument in this direction. Bostrom suggests that all technological innovations are a bit like picking random balls from a sack. Most things we discover are net-good (white balls), some are mixed (gray balls), while others are black. These black balls are innovations that are more or less entirely bad and potentially carry civilisation destroying consequences from simply being invented. I think the classical example of this would be anything that makes nukes relatively easy to obtain, but another, maybe more realistic example might be any technology which allows for the democratisation of advanced bio weapons (AI).

That said, I do also think AI alignment is fundamentally impossible too and something that's worth thinking about. We probably want AIs that won't start killing people because the US or Chinese governments tell them to go kill "the bad guys", but this means we want AIs that will ignore, and potentially block, the orders and actions of the most powerful incarnations of human government – effectively meaning we'd need to ceed ultimate power of our civilisations to the AIs. If you are good and you have the power to stop people killing each other, you should. If the AIs are good and war is bad, then they should stop us doing that.

So yeah, this is all reasonable. Obviously taking down a book isn't going to do much on its own, but any expert in the field raising concerns like this is good to see. Of course, we're all hoping the experts of HN are right and that the best thing would be if everyone had super advanced AIs running on their local machines. I suspect regardless of who is ultimately proven right this is where we're heading. I don't see how we stop the train at this point.

Moloch is basically the outcomes that nobody wants but that the systems we have built keep producing. Nobody designed it to do that. They just didn't design it not to.

It's basically the "anti-illuminati." Any time you see something that sucks, and makes no sense, it's logical to think "some asshole is making it suck, so we should just find him and get rid of him." In most cases, it's millions or billions of people doing that work. It's the whole ecosystem that produces that outcome.

(There are also actual cabals of course. The point is that there don't need to be, for things to suck. In our case we get both!)

I've heard it described as "emergent suck", the result of many "locally rational" actors each doing the thing that makes sense for them, producing globally horrifying outcomes.

For example, see Chicken Cage Simulator:

https://youtube.com/watch?v=b3y-snYz-h8

Nobody wanted to build Infinite Chicken Hell. They just wanted nuggets.

---

My favorite example is from my personal life. I was working at a food warehouse. Working conditions were not great. I constantly had managers breathing down my neck, and I was like, what is their problem? What the hell, why can't they just relax and let us work normally?

Well I realized, their managers are also breathing down their neck and so on. But where does that chain end? Do we have the fat capitalist with the monocle and the top hat at the end of it?

Well, maybe we do (something something shareholders?), but I realized something even more bizarre. What happens if they stop breathing down our necks, and actually let us work at a normal pace?

Well, everyone would work about 30 to 40% slower. The price of groceries would go up by similar amount. Grandma would probably stop buying from us. It might not fit in her budget anymore. She might switch to the competitor where the workers have to piss in bottles.

Grandma is Moloch.

---

Similar situation with AI and robotics. Let's say you run company. You employ humans. You want to continue employing humans.

Unfortunately your competitors begin employing machines, and they're able to provide the same product or service, let's say, a thousand times cheaper than you.

You still want to continue employing humans. But many of your customers will start wondering, why you are charging them a thousand times more than the guy next door. They may say they prefer companies staffed by humans instead of machines. But when asked to pay 100000% markup for the same service, their wallets may have a different opinion.

Average Joe is Moloch.

---

There are various defenses against Moloch. Religion is one — e.g. the Butlerian Jihad in Dune, or the religious laws around sexuality and caring for your parents that most religions have, which were widespread even in the west until quite recently. Regulation is another one. (e.g. banning robots from businesses, for example, so that people have no choice but to support human run businesses.)

Over thousands of years we have evolved, culturally, many, many defenses against Moloch, but spent the last two centuries or so systematically deleting them — the family, the church, the neighborhood, etc. — in the name of freedom and individualism. At this point, very few remain.

Technology is a powerful vector of Moloch. The Amish have solid defenses. But almost nobody wants to go that route. The next century or two are going to be very interesting. Looks like it's just going to be machines and Amish by the end of it!

Thanks for coming to my TED Talk!

It's not quite the same as that, because dumping toxic waste into a river adds pollution such that every little amount matters and directly harms additional organisms.

The risk of super-intelligence is much more binary. It either exists or it doesn't. If it doesn't exist, then we're not facing any sort of existential threat. But once it does exist, we are (potentially, but not necessarily) screwed.

So I think the better analogy is to compare it to a race. Only one party needs to cross the finish line, in order to bring something extremely dangerous into existence. Even if one party stops running, it doesn't change the fact that there are hundreds of others who are running, and anyone else can join the race at any point in time and do so in a way that can't possibly be policed.

As the lead runner, you're forced with the choice of (1) dropping out of the race, which will have just about as much effect as my pet hamster suddenly standing up and announcing that he's dropping out of the race. Remarkable and newsworthy, but it won't suddenly make the race un-winnable by someone else. Or, (2) trying to win the race, so at least it's you who possesses the dangerous power rather than someone else. Who knows, perhaps you can even use it to stop others from using it for evil.

So no, I don't think it's anything like the cumulative incremental process of dumping toxic wakes into a river. The closest analog is the nuclear arms race. If you're America, embedded in WW2, certain that WW3 is not long to follow, do you stop developing the atomic bomb and let the Germans or the Soviets do it?

Too black and white. Each separate effort at doing Y increases the chances of a catastrophe in this case. It's like saying that dumping toxic waste into a river is okay, because other people are already dumping toxic waste into other rivers.

This embodies an extremely naive view that nonetheless a lot of smart people hold: if person X believes Y could be very dangerous then they shouldn't do Y. It's completely naive, because X not doing Y will not make any difference if there are other people/groups who will do Y anyway. If there is no way to stop everyone from doing Y, then you're not adding additional danger to the world by working on it.

And I've never seen any realistic way that you could stop everyone from doing such work on AI. There's too much to be potentially gained from doing so, and there's too many people who don't believe that there actually is great risk to it (and by the way, I'm not one of them)

AND, if you work on it, you can try to make sure that it happens in the safest way possible. If you really think it is potentially dangerous, and there's no way to stop everyone from working on it, then the most responsible thing to do is probably to try to make it happen in the safest way possible.
